questions.stem: When is a relation in Domain–Key Normal Form (DKNF)?
options: When every constraint on the table can be expressed solely as a domain constraint or a key constraint
When every attribute has its own time-aware table
When every join dependency is implied by candidate keys
When every non-key attribute depends on the whole key
When no two independent multi-valued facts share a key
questions.explanation: A relation is in DKNF if every constraint can be expressed solely as either a domain constraint or a key constraint; any other rule means it is not in DKNF.

questions.stem: What does a domain constraint define?
options: Which combination of attributes uniquely identifies a row
What values are valid for a column
How tables are joined together
Which table owns a foreign key
The order in which rows are stored
questions.explanation: A domain constraint governs permissible values, for example a DecisionStatus column allowing only APPROVED, REJECTED or PENDING.

questions.stem: What does a key constraint define?
options: Valid values for a column
The data type of a column
Uniqueness: which combination of attributes uniquely identifies a row
Whether a column may be null
The validity period of a fact
questions.explanation: A key constraint specifies which combination of attributes uniquely identifies a row, such as LoanID for a loan or (LoanID, EffectiveStart) for a time-bound fact.

questions.stem: Why does the rule "If a loan is APPROVED, it must have a RepaymentSchedule" prevent a schema from reaching Domain–Key Normal Form?
options: Because it is a domain constraint on the wrong column
Because it is a key constraint on a composite key
Because APPROVED is not a valid domain value
Because it is a cross-table conditional rule that is neither purely a domain constraint nor purely a key constraint
Because repayment schedules cannot be modelled relationally
questions.explanation: The rule is not about valid values nor about uniqueness; it is a cross-table conditional rule, so unless the schema enforces it structurally the relation is not in DKNF.

questions.stem: Why do most real-world schemas not reach Domain–Key Normal Form?
options: Because databases do not support domain constraints
Because DKNF requires more tables than 6NF
Because DKNF forbids composite keys
Because DKNF only applies to NoSQL systems
Because many business rules are conditional or cross-entity and need triggers, application logic or procedural enforcement
questions.explanation: Many business rules are conditional or span entities and require triggers, application logic or procedural enforcement beyond simple domain and key constraints.

questions.stem: Between which normal forms do most practical systems stabilise?
options: Between 3NF and BCNF, occasionally extending to 4NF or 6NF
Between 1NF and 2NF
Between 5NF and DKNF
Always at 6NF
Always at DKNF
questions.explanation: In practical architecture most systems stabilise between 3NF and BCNF, occasionally extending to 4NF or 6NF in specialised cases.

questions.stem: According to the comparison of normalisation with specialised modelling techniques, how does dimensional modelling relate to normal forms?
options: It requires 5NF or 6NF for accuracy
It is the opposite: intentional denormalisation for analytical performance
It is explicitly grounded in 6NF principles
Normalisation is not applicable because it predates the relational model
It satisfies DKNF by design
questions.explanation: Dimensional models such as star, snowflake and USS are designed for analytical performance and intentionally introduce redundancy for faster queries.

questions.stem: Which modelling technique is described as explicitly grounded in 6NF-style decomposition and temporal principles?
options: Hierarchical modelling
Event-driven modelling
Anchor Modelling
API / service modelling
Object-oriented modelling
questions.explanation: Anchor Modelling is the technique marked as explicitly grounded in 6NF-style decomposition and temporal principles, whereas Data Vault and Focal Point are only related.

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques is NOT listed as one where normalisation theory is simply not applicable?
options: Hierarchical and network modelling
Object-oriented modelling
NoSQL modelling
Data Vault modelling
Event-driven modelling
questions.explanation: Data Vault is marked as related to normalisation because its satellites resemble 6NF-style decomposition; the others are marked as not applicable.

questions.stem: What is the central question that changes when moving from foundational normalisation to specialised modelling techniques?
options: From "Which database vendor?" to "Which cloud platform?"
From "How many tables?" to "How many rows?"
From "Is the key composite?" to "Is the key surrogate?"
From "Is the data atomic?" to "Is the data historical?"
From "Is the model fully normalised?" to "What problem is this model designed to solve?"
questions.explanation: Layer #4 shifts perspective from foundational relational rigour to purposeful specialisation, asking what problem a model is designed to solve rather than whether it is fully normalised.
